lesson.title: Rebase a Feature Branch onto Main and Resolve Conflicts
lesson.goal: rebase a feature branch onto main with git and resolve the conflicts

goalMatch.note: This video covers exactly what you asked: how to rebase a branch with git and how to resolve conflicts during the rebase, with a worked example.

sources.title: Rebase a Feature Branch onto Main and Resolve Conflicts

steps.title: Rebase feature branch onto main
steps.instructions: In the empty lesson folder run `git init -b main`, commit a file, create `feature` with `git switch -c feature` and commit a change to a different file, then switch to main and commit. Switch to `feature`, run `git rebase main`, and check `git log --oneline --graph` for a linear history.

targets.caption: Rebase the feature branch onto main

explanations.topic: Rebasing avoids an extra merge commit
Commits set aside and reapplied on top of main
Why it's called rebasing: new base commit

hints: Make sure you are on the feature branch (git switch feature) before rebasing.
main needs a commit that feature doesn't have, so commit on main after creating feature.
Edit different files on each branch so the rebase doesn't conflict.
Run git log --oneline --graph: every line should start with '*' and have no branching '|\' lines.
common_mistakes: Running git rebase main while still on main, so nothing happens.
Running git merge main instead of rebase, which creates a merge commit.
Editing the same file on both branches, causing a conflict in this step.
Forgetting to commit on main after creating feature, so the rebase reports 'Current branch feature is up to date'.
steps.code:
git init -b main
git add . && git commit -m "initial commit"
git switch -c feature
# edit a different file
git commit -am "feature work"
git switch main
# edit a file
git commit -am "main work"
git switch feature
git rebase main
git log --oneline --graph

steps.title: Check branch is unpushed
steps.instructions: Run `git branch -a` to list local and remote branches. Only rebase if your feature branch has no `remotes/...` entry.

targets.caption: Local branches; any remotes/ entry for your feature branch means it was pushed
The asterisk marks the branch you're currently on

explanations.topic: Golden rule: never rebase commits you've already pushed
Rebasing changes commit hashes, so local and remote no longer match
Why this hurts teammates who already pulled, and why merge doesn't have this problem
Use git branch -a to check whether the feature branch exists on the remote

hints: Run git branch -a inside your repository to list both local and remote-tracking branches.
Remote branches show up with a remotes/ prefix, e.g. remotes/origin/<name>.
If your feature branch has a remotes/... entry, it's already pushed. Don't rebase it. If it has none, rebasing is safe.
common_mistakes: Running plain git branch (no -a), which hides remote branches, so a pushed branch looks unpushed.
Running the command outside the repository folder and getting 'fatal: not a git repository'.
Using a stale view of the remote. Run git fetch first if teammates may have pushed the branch.
Rebasing a branch that is listed under remotes/ and then force-pushing over teammates' work.

steps.title: Set up conflicting repo, start rebase
steps.instructions: Create `feature/login` from main with three commits where commits 1 and 3 edit the same line of `login.txt` that two new commits on main also change, while commit 2 edits a separate file. On `feature/login` run `git rebase main`, then `git status` to confirm the rebase is paused on a conflict.

precision_checks.label: Rebase is paused
precision_checks.command: test -d "$(git rev-parse --git-path rebase-merge)" || test -d "$(git rev-parse --git-path rebase-apply)"

targets.caption: The rebase stopped on the first conflicting commit
git status confirms the rebase is paused
The conflicted file waiting for your fix

explanations.topic: Rebase reapplies commits one by one, so each can conflict
Repo layout: three feature commits off an older main commit, two new main commits
Why commits 1 and 3 conflict but the middle one doesn't
Rebase pauses on conflict; git status shows progress and remaining commits
Resolving rebase conflicts works like merge conflicts: remove markers, keep the right code, git add

hints: Make the feature branch from main first, then add your three commits. Afterwards switch back to main and add the two commits that change the same line.
Commits 1 and 3 on the feature branch and both new main commits should edit the same line of login.txt. Commit 2 should touch a different file.
Run `git switch feature/login`, then `git rebase main`. When it stops on a conflict, run `git status`.
git status should say a rebase is in progress and list login.txt under 'both modified'. Don't fix the conflict yet.
common_mistakes: Running `git rebase main` while still on main instead of on feature/login.
Editing different lines in the main and feature commits, so the rebase finishes without any conflict.
Adding the main commits before branching, so the feature branch already contains them.
Running `git rebase --abort` or resolving the conflict too early, so the paused state is gone.
steps.code:
git switch feature/login
git rebase main
git status

steps.title: Resolve conflict and continue
steps.instructions: Open the file git reports as CONFLICT, remove the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers keeping the correct code, then `git add` it. Run `git rebase --continue` and in Vim press Escape and type `:wq` to keep the message.

targets.caption: Continue the rebase after git add
Save and quit Vim to keep the message

explanations.topic: Use git rebase --continue instead of committing
Vim opens for the commit message; Esc then :wq saves and quits

hints: Open the file git listed as conflicted and search for <<<<<<<.
Delete the three marker lines (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) and keep only the code that should stay, then save.
Stage the file with git add <file>, then run git rebase --continue (not git commit).
When Vim opens, press Escape, type :wq and press Enter to keep the commit message.
common_mistakes: Leaving a marker line such as ======= or >>>>>>> in the file.
Running git commit instead of git rebase --continue.
Forgetting to git add the resolved file before continuing.
Getting stuck in Vim: typing :wq without pressing Escape first, or typing it while in insert mode.
Keeping both sides of the conflict when only one should remain.
steps.code:
# remove the <<<<<<< HEAD, ======= and >>>>>>> markers, keep the correct code
git add <conflicted-file>
git rebase --continue
# in Vim: Esc, then :wq

steps.title: Fix second conflict, finish rebase
steps.instructions: Resolve the next conflict the same way, `git add` the file and run `git rebase --continue`. Run `git status` to confirm the rebase is finished.

targets.caption: git status shows a normal branch

explanations.topic: Non-conflicting commits are applied automatically during a rebase
Rebase pauses again at each conflicting commit
Using git status to confirm the rebase is finished

hints: Git paused again because the third commit conflicts. Fix it the same way you fixed the first conflict.
Open the conflicting file, keep the lines you want, and delete the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers.
Stage the resolved file with git add <file>, then run git rebase --continue and close the commit-message editor.
Run git status. It should say 'On branch ...' with no 'rebase in progress' message.
common_mistakes: Leaving conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) in the file before running git add
Running git commit instead of git rebase --continue
Forgetting to git add the resolved file, so --continue complains about unmerged paths
Not saving and closing the commit-message editor (e.g. Vim :wq), so the rebase looks stuck
Running git rebase --abort by mistake, which undoes all the progress
steps.run_command: git add <file> && git rebase --continue && git status
